translation_credits: Provisional English game glosses drafted in-house for this class project with AI assistance (Claude), 2026-11-28. Glosses for the 30 pilot poems are reused verbatim from data/genji_poetry_exchanges_pilot.json. Not taken from any published translation. Not reviewed by a specialist.
style: One plain prose sentence per poem. Keeps the poem's images, and where a linked partner shares a hook word, uses the same English word in both. Notes explain puns that English cannot carry; they are shown only after the answer.

glosses.english: Now that we reach the end and part on separate roads, how sad it is: the road I long to take is the road of life.
Hearing the wind that binds the dew on Miyagi Moor, my thoughts go out to the young bush clover beneath it.
glosses.note: The young bush clover (kohagi) is the motherless child, Genji.

glosses.english: Though the bell-cricket, that autumn insect, sings until its voice gives out, the long night is not long enough for my falling tears.
To this patch of reeds already loud with insect cries, a visitor from above the clouds adds yet more dew of tears.
Since the tree that sheltered it from the harsh wind has withered, my heart cannot rest for the young bush clover.
glosses.note: Answers poem 2: the sheltering tree is the dead mother.

glosses.english: If only there were a wizard who could search her out, so that even by hearsay I might learn where her spirit dwells.
Even above the clouds the autumn moon is dark with tears; how could it shine clearly on that reed-grown house?
Into this first hair-cord of his boyhood, did you tie a pledge that your line and his will be bound forever?
If the deep purple of the hair-cord I have tied with all my heart does not fade, our bond will hold.
Counting on my fingers the times we have met, is this truly the only painful turn in your dealings with me?
I have counted those painful turns alone in my heart; is this the moment when your own hand will let go of mine?
A house where koto music and moonlight are so fine: could even these hold back a man so cold?
glosses.note: Koto (koto) also means 'words'.

glosses.english: With the cold wind blowing along with your flute, I have no koto, no word, fit to hold you back.
glosses.note: Koto (koto) also means 'words'.

glosses.english: Though the mountain hedge is humble, now and then let your pity fall like dew on the little pink.
glosses.note: The pink (nadeshiko, 'stroked child') is their daughter.

glosses.english: I cannot tell which of these mingled blossoms is fairest, but none surpasses the everlasting pink.
glosses.note: Tokonatsu, 'everlasting summer', is another name for the pink and puns on the bed (toko).

glosses.english: Even the sleeves that brush the bed of the everlasting pink are wet with dew, and now the autumn storm blows too.
At dusk, when the spider's weaving shows that you will come, how strange to tell me to wait out the garlic-reeking daytime.
glosses.note: Hiruma plays on 'daytime' and the garlic (hiru) she has eaten.

glosses.english: If ours were a bond that met every night, why should even the garlic-reeking daytime be too bright for you?
Before I can finish my complaint at your coldness, dawn comes, and the cock's crow hurries me away.
While I still lament my wretched lot, the night grows light, and with the cock's crow I sob all the more.
Grieving whether I will ever again have a night to meet you as in that dream, I have spent these days without closing my eyes.
Not knowing the heart of the broom tree of Sonohara, I have wandered lost upon the road to it.
glosses.note: The broom tree (hahakigi) is seen from afar but vanishes as one approaches.

glosses.english: Ashamed of the name of one born in a humble hut, I vanish like the broom tree, neither here nor there.
Beneath the tree where the cicada changed its body, I still find the empty shell of that person dear.
glosses.note: Utsusemi, 'cicada shell', is the robe she left behind.

glosses.english: Like dew settling on a cicada's wing, hidden among the trees, my sleeves grow wet with secret tears.
I can only guess that it is you: the evening-face flower shines more brightly beneath the pale dew.
Only coming closer could I tell if it is truly you, the evening-face blossom I glimpsed faintly in twilight.
Though I fear being called one who shifts to every blooming flower, I can hardly pass this morning glory by unpicked.
Since you leave before the morning mist even clears, it seems your heart has not settled on the flower.
Following the path the lay monk walks in prayer, do not break our vow, deep enough to last into the next life.
Knowing from my sorrows how poor my vows in a past life were, I can hardly trust in what is to come.
Did others in the past lose their way like this? I have never known such a road at dawn.
Not knowing the heart of the mountain rim it goes toward, the moon in the empty sky may fade away midway.
The flower opening in the evening dew: it was our bond that let me see it by the roadside.
glosses.note: Genji uncovers his face to Yūgao.

glosses.english: The dew on the evening face that seemed to shine so brightly was only a trick of the twilight eye.
When I gaze on the clouds as the smoke of the one I lost, even the evening sky feels dear to me.
While time passes and you never ask why I do not ask after you, how tangled my thoughts have grown.
I knew this cicada-shell world was full of sorrow, yet once again my life hangs on your words.
Had I not tied even faintly the reed by the eaves, on what would I hang my complaint of dew?
At the faint wind you send, the low reed by the eaves is half bound up in frost.
Weeping as I tie this sash for parting today, in what life will I see it loosened again?
I kept your robe as a keepsake until we met again, but my sleeves have rotted through with tears.
Seeing the summer robe returned, changed as the cicada changes its wings, I can only weep aloud.
The one who has passed and the one who leaves today go by two roads I cannot follow, at autumn's end.
Not knowing where this young grass will grow to maturity, the dew that shelters it cannot bear to vanish.
Before you know where the new grass will grow, how can the dew think of disappearing?
Ever since I glimpsed the new grass with its young leaves, my traveler's sleeves have not been dry of dew.
Do not compare the dew that wets your pillow for one night with the moss of these deep mountains.
Woken from my dream by the wind blowing down the mountain, I am moved to tears by the sound of the falls.
You wet your sleeves at once in the mountain water, but a heart that has settled here is not stirred by its falls.
I will go and tell the courtiers of these mountain cherries: come see them before the wind does.
I feel as though I have found the rare udumbara in bloom; my eyes do not turn to the mountain cherries now.
Opening at last my pine door deep in the mountains, I see a face like a flower I have never seen.
Having glimpsed the flower's color faintly at dusk, this morning the mist is loath to rise and go.
Is it true that it is hard to rise and leave the flower? Let me watch the misted sky to see.
The image of the mountain cherry never leaves me; I left my whole heart behind with it.
How fleeting, to leave your heart with the mountain cherry on the peak while the storm has yet to scatter it.
My feelings are not shallow like Mount Asaka's spring; why does the mountain well keep its reflection from me?
I have heard of those who regret drawing from the mountain well; could I let you see its reflection while it is so shallow?
Meeting you again is as rare as a night in a dream; I wish I could vanish into that dream.
Will people pass on our story, even if I make my wretched self a dream that never wakes?
Since I heard the young crane's single cry, my boat stuck among the reeds cannot go on.
When can I pick and hold the young grass of the moor whose root runs to the purple plant?
glosses.note: Murasaki ('purple') is Fujitsubo's niece; the grass is the girl.

glosses.english: Though seaweed is hard to find in Waka Bay, will the wave go back without even rising to it?
To let the jeweled seaweed of Waka Bay drift with the wave without knowing its heart would be rash.
Even lost in the misty morning sky, I find it hard to pass my lady's gate.
If you find it so hard to pass the misty hedge, the grass door would not have kept you out.
Though I have not slept with it, I love the grass of Musashi Moor, kin to the one I long for, wet with dew.
glosses.note: The 'kin grass' (kusa no yukari) is Murasaki, Fujitsubo's niece.

glosses.english: I do not know why you should sigh; what grass could I be kin to?
We left the palace together, yet you hide where you set, like the sixteenth-night moon.
The moon's light falls on every house alike; who would follow it to the mountain where it sets?
How many times have I lost to your silence, trusting that you did not say 'Do not speak'?
The bell has rung to end the silence; I cannot answer, and yet it is strange to say nothing.
I know that not speaking can say more than speech, but such held-in silence is painful.
Before I have even seen the evening mist clear, the night rain adds to my gloom.
Think of my village, waiting for the moon on a night that will not clear, even if you do not share my gazing.
The icicles on the eaves melt in the morning sun; why then does the ice stay frozen here?
Seeing the snow on the old man's head, my morning sleeves are as wet as his.
Because your heart is cold, the sleeves of this Chinese robe are always wet with tears.
Its color is not one I love; why did I let this safflower brush my sleeve?
glosses.note: Suetsumuhana, 'safflower', also points to her red nose.

glosses.english: Even if the red safflower robe is thinly dyed, do not ruin its name entirely.
Do you send me robes to layer, so that I may look still more on the nights we spend apart?
The red flower is somehow unpleasing, though the tall plum branch is dear.
glosses.note: Red flower (hana) also means 'nose'.

glosses.english: Did you understand my heart as I waved my sleeves, in no state to dance for all my longing?
The waving of sleeves by men of China is far from me, yet I watched every movement with feeling.
What bond did we tie in some past life, that this barrier lies between us in this one?
She who sees him grieves; how much more must you who do not see him lament, lost in the darkness of a parent's heart.
Comparing it with him brings my heart no comfort; the dew on the little pink only grows heavier.
Though I think of it as kin to the dew that wets my sleeves, I still cannot turn from the Yamato pink.
If you come, I will feed grass to your tamed colt, though the lower leaves are past their prime.
If I pushed through the bamboo grass, people would blame me: your grove is always full of colts.
No one comes to stand and get wet at my eastern cottage; how hateful this falling rain.
Another man's wife is trouble; I would not grow too familiar with the eaves of your eastern cottage.
Pulling at each other, our name will leak out like rain through the torn sleeves of the robe between us.
Knowing it will all come out, you wear a summer robe; I see your heart is thin as it.
There is no use complaining after the waves that rose one on another and rolled back.
My heart is not troubled by the waves that rose wildly, but how could I not resent the shore they came to?
Afraid I'll be blamed if our tie is broken, I won't even take back the indigo sash.
Since the sash you pulled from me is now yours, I will blame you that our tie is broken.
I am lost in the endless darkness of a parent's heart as I see her above the clouds.
If I could see the flower's beauty as others do, would the dew of feeling settle on my heart?
That you too know the beauty of the deep night with its setting moon must be no common bond.
If I, poor thing, should vanish from this world, would you not seek me out on the grassy moor?
While I try to tell which blade the dew has settled on, the wind may blow across the bamboo-grass moor.
I feel as never before, having lost the dawn moon's path across the sky.
If the blossoms at my house were of the common sort, why would I wait for you to come?
I wander lost on Mount Irusa, wondering if I'll see again the moon I glimpsed so faintly.
glosses.note: Azusa-yumi, 'catalpa bow', leads to iru, 'shoot' and 'enter'.

glosses.english: If your heart truly aimed there, would you lose your way under a sky with no bow-shaped moon?
Glimpsing only his reflection in the cold Mitarashi River, I learn all the more how wretched I am.
I alone will watch the deep seaweed of the endless thousand-fathom bottom grow.
glosses.note: The seaweed is Murasaki's hair, which Genji is trimming.

glosses.english: How could you know its thousand fathoms, when the tide that ebbs and flows is never still?
How futile to have waited for the god's sanctioned day, just for the aoi leaves another person wears—the day of meeting.
glosses.note: Aoi (heartvine) puns on au hi, 'day of meeting'.

glosses.english: The heart that placed those leaves in the hair seems fickle to me—offering an aoi, a day of meeting, to every courtier alike.
How I regret having worn them in my hair: mere leaves of grass that promise a meeting in name only.
Knowing full well that the path of love soaks the sleeves, I step down into its muddy field myself, to my sorrow.
glosses.note: Koiji puns on 'path of love' and 'muddy field'.

glosses.english: You step only into the shallows, while I am soaked to the skin in the deep mud of the path of love.
Tie fast my soul that wanders the sky in grief, binding the hem of your robe in the old charm.
I cannot tell which rising smoke is hers, yet the whole sky of clouds is full of sorrow.
Custom keeps my mourning robe pale, yet my tears have turned its sleeves into deep pools.
Hearing of the world's sorrows wets my sleeves with dew; I think of the sleeves of one left behind.
Those who stay and those who vanish are alike in this world of dew; how vain to set the heart on it, left behind.
She has become rain; in this sky of drizzling, drifting clouds, how can I tell which one is hers?
Even the sky where she became rain and cloud is darkened more by the autumn drizzle.
I see the pink left by the withered hedge as a keepsake of the autumn when she left.
Looking at it now only rots my sleeves with tears, the Yamato pink in a ruined hedge.
My sleeves are wetter with dew this evening than in all the autumns of sorrow I have passed.
Since I heard you were left behind in the autumn mist, I have wondered how you bear this drizzling sky.
The departed soul is all the sadder, for this bed we shared was one it could hardly leave.
Without you, how many nights have I brushed the dew from the everlasting pink, where dust has piled?
How senseless that we kept apart so long, though our night robes were long familiar.
After so many years I put on these colors renewed for today, and my tears fall as if it were the old days.
New year or not, what falls is the tears of one grown old.
The sacred fence has no cedar to mark the way; why did you break this sakaki branch by mistake?
Thinking the shrine maiden near, I loved the scent of the sakaki leaves and broke a branch to stay.
Dawn partings are always wet with dew, but this one is under an autumn sky unknown to the world.
An autumn parting is sad enough; pine cricket of the moor, do not add your crying.
Gods of the land who guard these isles, if you have hearts, judge between us, parting unwilling.
If the gods of the land are to judge between you in the sky, they will first examine your empty words.
I resolved not to speak of the past today, yet in my heart there is sorrow.
Though you shake me off and go today, will your sleeves not be wet in the eighty shallows of the Suzuka River?
Whether or not my sleeves are wet in the eighty shallows of the Suzuka River, who will send his thoughts after me to Ise?
I will keep gazing the way you went; this autumn, mist, do not hide Ōsaka Mountain.
Has the pine whose broad shade we trusted withered? Its lower leaves fall as the year ends.
In the cold clear mirror of the pond, I grieve not to see the reflection I knew so well.
As the year ends the rock-spring water freezes, and the reflection of one we knew fades away.
I wet my sleeves by my own fault, hearing a voice that tells me dawn has come.
glosses.note: Aku means both 'dawn breaks' and 'grow tired'.

glosses.english: Must I pass my life in sighs like this, with never a time my heart can dawn and be eased?
If today is not the last of these hard meetings, how many more lives must I spend in sighs?
Even if you leave resentment to last through a long life, know that the fault is your own fickle heart.
Having left you in the dewy lodging of the reeds, I cannot rest for the winds blowing on every side.
When the wind blows, the spider web hanging from the reeds' fading dew is the first to tremble.
It may be presumptuous even to speak of it, yet the sacred shoulder-cord draws my mind back to that god—and to old times.
glosses.note: Sono kami means both 'that god' and 'that time'.

glosses.english: What was that god—or that former time—to you, that you should keep the ritual cord tied in your thoughts and long for it?
Does mist divide the nine-fold palace? I think of the moon above the clouds from far away.
The moonlight is no different from the autumn nights we knew, but how cruel is the mist that divides us.
Waiting as each cold wind blows, I have spent these days in doubt.
Do you think the tears I shed in these days of secret longing are only the sky's common drizzle?
Today, the day of parting, ends; when can I hope to meet again the one I knew?
Though living on is hard, coming round today again, I feel I meet that time once more.
Though I long to follow you to the clouds where the moon shines clear, I am still lost in this world's darkness.
I shun this world for its many sorrows, but when can I turn from this world entirely?
Seeing this as the home of a nun, my tears drip like brine at Matsugaura Island.
glosses.note: Ama means both 'nun' and 'fisher'.

glosses.english: How rare, the waves that come to the island bay where nothing remains of the past.
In this morning's first-opened flower I see your beauty, no less fragrant than it.
The flower that bloomed out of season this morning wilts in the summer rain, with no fragrance left.
The cuckoo returns, unable to hold back, to the hedge where it once sang softly.
The cuckoo's voice that calls is the same, but how uncertain is this sky of early-summer rain.
Drawn by the orange blossom's scent, the cuckoo seeks out the village of falling flowers.
At this ruined house where no one comes, only the orange blossom draws you to the eaves.
I go to the shore where fishers burn salt, as if to mingle with the smoke that rose on Toribe Hill.
Will you not go further still from the one who died, outside the sky where she became smoke?
Though I wander like this, my reflection will not leave the mirror that stays by you.
If at least your reflection would stay when we part, I could take comfort looking in the mirror.
Narrow though my sleeve is where the moonlight lodges, I wish I could keep its light, of which I never tire.
Coming round, the moonlight will shine clear at last; do not gaze at a sky clouded for a while.
Did I sink in the river of tears, with no shallows to meet you, as the first step of drifting away?
The foam floating on the river of tears will surely vanish without waiting to meet again in the shallows.
One I knew is gone, one who lives is sad; at the world's end, what use was turning from it but to weep and weep?
I thought the sorrow of parting was exhausted, but the pain of this world grows worse.
Remembering that day we wore aoi together in our hair, how cruel is the Kamo shrine's sacred fence.
I leave this world of sorrow now; I leave my name to the god of Tadasu to judge.
How does your departed spirit see me? The moon I gaze at, thinking of you, is hidden in clouds.
When will I see the flowers of the spring capital again, a mountain peasant who has lost his time?
It is hard that flowers fall so soon, but come back and look on the flowers of the capital in a passing spring.
I pledged my life to you, not knowing there are partings while we live.
I would give my worthless life to hold back for a while this parting before my eyes.
Rather than leave a name in China like the exiles there, I may simply vanish without trace.
Mist on the peaks hides my old home, but is not the sky I gaze at the same sky?
How is it with the fisher-nun's hut at Matsushima, while this man of Suma Bay drips brine?
Unrepentant, I long for the seaweed of Suma Bay; what does the fisher who burns salt there think?
glosses.note: Mirume, 'seaweed', also means 'a chance to meet'.

glosses.english: The fisher-nun at Matsushima, long years dripping brine as her task, piles up her sighs like wood.
My love is hidden among the many fishers' fires on the bay; the smoke smolders with nowhere to go.
Compare the sleeves of the bay folk, wet with brine, to my night robe, kept apart from you by the waves.
Think of the fisher of Ise, gathering wretched seaweed, as you drip brine at Suma Bay.
glosses.note: Ukime is both 'floating seaweed' and 'misery'.

glosses.english: Though I search the brine-wet beach of Ise for shells, the one with no worth left is me.
glosses.note: Kai is 'shell' and 'worth'.

glosses.english: I would have boarded the little boat rowing the waves of Ise, rather than gather wretched seaweed here.
Dripping brine among the fisher's piled sighs, how long must I gaze out over Suma Bay?
Gazing at the fern of longing growing thick on the ruined eaves, my sleeves are heavy with dew.
The waves of the bay seem to echo my sobs of longing; does the wind blow from where my love is?
Are the first wild geese companions of the one I love? How sad their voices crossing the traveler's sky.
Thoughts of old times come in a line, though the wild geese were never our friends in those days.
I used to think of the wild geese crying beyond the clouds, who left their eternal land by choice.
Even the wild geese, leaving their eternal land for the traveler's sky, take comfort in not falling behind their line.
Only while I gaze am I comforted; the capital of the moon, where we will meet again, is far away.
Thinking only of sorrow, I find my sleeves wet on the left and on the right.
If the koto's sound holds me back like a towline, would you know how my heart hangs in hesitation?
If the rope pulling your boat truly wavered out of feeling, could it simply pass beyond the waves of Suma?
Come visit, friends from home I long for, as often as the brushwood burns in this peasant's hut.
On which cloud path will I too be lost? I am ashamed of what the moon will see.
At dawn, when plovers cry in chorus, even a bed of waking alone is a comfort.
Always longing for the courtiers of the palace, the day we wore cherry blossoms in our hair has come again.
In which spring will I go and see my old home? How I envy the wild geese going back.
Unwilling, I leave the wild geese's temporary home; will I lose my way on the road to the flower capital?
glosses.note: Kari is both 'wild goose' and 'temporary'.

glosses.english: Look into the sky, you cranes flying near the clouds: I am one without a cloud, like a spring day.
Helpless, I cry alone in the clouds like a crane, longing for the friend I flew beside.
Washed up on an ocean I never knew, is it only one thing that makes me sad?
The myriad gods must surely pity me, for I have committed no particular crime.
How does the bay wind blow? My sleeves are wet with thinking of you in these days of endless waves.
Without the help of the god who dwells in the sea, I would have drifted among the meeting tides.
I think of you from far away, having followed the shore beyond the bay I never knew.
Even the pathos of Awaji Island, seen faintly, is lit without a shadow by the clear night moon.
Do you know now too what it is to sleep alone, lonely all night long by the Akashi shore?
glosses.note: Akashi puns on akasu, 'to stay up until dawn'.

glosses.english: In my traveler's robe, too sad by the shore to stay up till dawn at Akashi, I cannot even dream on my grass pillow.
Gazing sadly at a distant sky I do not know, I write to the treetops of the house I heard of.
She who gazes at the same distant sky that you gaze at must surely have the same thoughts.
How gloomy my troubled heart, with no one to ask me, 'Well, and how are you?'
'Well, and how are you?' How deep can your feelings be, troubled over one you have never seen?
Moon-grey colt of the autumn night, fly across the sky to the one I love, so I may see her for a moment.
If only I had someone with whom to share intimate words—perhaps I might wake halfway from this bitter world's dream.
My heart is lost in a night that never dawns; how could I tell which part is dream and put it into words?
Dripping brine, I weep first of all, waiting like the pine; would the waves cross over? My glimpse of the seaweed was only a fisher's pastime.
glosses.note: Matsu is 'pine' and 'wait'; mirume, 'seaweed', is also 'a chance to meet'.

glosses.english: How trusting I was, believing our vow, that the waves would never cross over the Pine Hill.
glosses.note: Matsu is 'pine' and 'wait'; waves crossing the pine hill is an old image of broken faith.

glosses.english: Though we part on this journey, the salt-burning smoke will drift the same way as yours.
Gathering my thoughts like the fishers' salt-burning seaweed, I will not even resent you now, when it is useless.
Shall I keep on longing, sounding my endless sobs, for the single word you left so lightly?
Let the tuning of the middle string we pledged as a keepsake until we meet never change.
How sad to leave you behind; I wonder how the bay waves will feel when they ebb away.
My rush hut of many years will fall to ruin; I would go with the sad waves back where they return.
Will you shun this traveler's robe I have layered for you, rising like night waves, as damp with brine?
Let us exchange robes as keepsakes; this robe will lie between us through the days until we meet.
Weary of the world, my body steeped in brine, I still cannot leave this shore.
Could my grief in spring on leaving the capital be less than this autumn, leaving the bay of many years?
Like the leech child of the sea who could not stand, I have passed the years drooping and forlorn.
glosses.note: An allusion to the myth of Izanagi and Izanami's first child.

glosses.english: Since we have met again like the gods circling the pillar, leave behind your resentment of that parting spring.
Sighing, I think of you on the Akashi shore, wondering whether the morning mist rises there.
I would show the boatman whose heart drew near to Suma's bay the sleeves he has left to rot.
Should I be the one to complain? My sleeves, too, have hardly dried since the waves drew you near.
Though we were never accustomed to an intimacy without distance, I have learned that parting is painful all the same.
Is your sudden lament at parting only a pretext, so that you may follow wherever your heart truly wishes to go?
When can I cover her with my sleeves, the maiden whose future grows like rock stroked by angels' sleeves over ages?
Stroking her alone, my sleeves are too small; I wait for a shade wide enough to cover her.
Even if we do not lean the same way, I would rather go first as smoke.
For whose sake did I wander sea and mountain, sinking and floating in endless tears?
Living in the shade of the sea pine where no season comes, how can the child tell the iris festival?
Hidden among the islands, a crane of no account cries, and today again no one asks how she is.
If not even the water rail came knocking, how would the moon be let into this ruined house?
If you open to every water rail that knocks, a wandering moon may slip in as well.
The pines of Sumiyoshi move me most, when I think of the age of gods.
Could I ever forget the god of Sumiyoshi, whom I called on amid the wild waves?
Our bond must be deep, to bring us together even here, marked like the channel posts by my longing.
glosses.note: Miotsukushi is a channel marker and 'giving one's whole self'.

glosses.english: I am of no account, and nothing at Naniwa is worth it; why did I give my whole self, like a channel post, to love you?
This traveler's robe is damp as in the old days; the isle of Tamino gives me no shelter.
How sad this house, in a sky of falling snow and rain without a break, where her spirit must be soaring.
How sad that I live on, unable to vanish, in a falling darkness where I hardly know myself.
The jeweled vine I trusted never to break has, against my hopes, drifted far away.
Even if the jeweled vine breaks, I will not leave you; I swear by the gods of the road I take.
My sleeves, wet with longing for the dead, are never dry, and the drip from the ruined eaves adds more.
I will be the one to seek you out, though there is no path through the deep mugwort, to find your heart unchanged.
I could hardly pass by these waves of wisteria; they must be the sign of a house that has waited for me.
glosses.note: Matsu is 'pine' and 'wait'.

glosses.english: For years my house has waited without a sign of reward; have you only stopped by because the flowers gave you a reason?
Will people see my tears, which I cannot hold back as I come and go, as the barrier's endless spring?
I trusted in our rare meeting on the road, but it was no use: a sea without salt.
glosses.note: Kai is 'shellfish' and 'worth'; a freshwater lake has none.

glosses.english: What kind of barrier is the Barrier of Meeting, that it divides us through such thick sighs?
Did the god forbid us, with the comb I gave at our parting, to be kept so far apart?
Even the word you spoke so far away when I parted now turns back to sorrow.
Rather than sigh alone, I should have seen the fishers' shore you lived on, like this.
Today the tears flow back to the past even more than when I saw misery there.
Without fathoming the deep heart of the Ise sea, should the waves wash out the old traces as worn?
To a heart that rises above the clouds, even a thousand-fathom bottom looks far away.
The seaweed of the bay may look old, but should the name of the Ise fisher of many years be sunk?
Though I am outside the sacred rope now, I have not forgotten the heart of that time, that god.
Within the sacred rope it no longer feels as before; now I long even for the days of the gods.
On this parting road, praying for your far future, what never ends is an old man's tears.
We left the capital together; on this journey, will I lose my way alone in the fields?
When can we meet again alive? How can I trust a world whose end I do not know?
The fisher's boat whose heart was drawn to the far shore rows back to the coast it left.
Having seen so many autumns come and go, I row back now aboard a drifting log.
glosses.note: Ukigi, 'floating log', also suggests uki, 'sorrow'.

glosses.english: Changed, I return alone to this mountain village, where the pine wind blows as it did by the sea.
Who can understand what I play, longing for the friend I knew in my old home?
The one who lived here returns and gropes for the old ways, while the spring acts as master of the house.
The little spring has not forgotten the past; has the old master changed his face?
In this tuning unchanged since our vow, did you know how unbroken my heart has been?
Trusting your vow that nothing would change, I added my sobs to the pine wind's sound.
A village across the river where the moon shines clear must have a calm light from the moon-laurel.
glosses.note: Katsura is both the laurel in the moon and the place name.

glosses.english: Katsura has only the name of being near the light; mist hangs morning and evening on this mountain village.
Come round again, the moon I saw faintly at Awaji Island is now so clear I could hold it.
The moonlight, hidden a while by drifting clouds, will be calm now that it shines clear for good.
Leaving its dwelling above the clouds, into which valley did the midnight moon hide its light?
Though the mountain road is buried in deep snow, keep coming, do not let your tracks be lost.
Even seeking her in the snowbound Yoshino mountains, could the tracks of hearts that reach out ever be lost?
Parted from the young pine of two leaves with its long future, when will I see its tall shade?
Its roots run deep from its first growth; the little pine will stand a thousand years beside the pine of Takekuma.
If there were no one on the far shore to stop your boat, I could wait for you to return tomorrow.
I will go and see, and come back tomorrow without fail, even if the one on the far shore resents it.
Do the thin clouds trailing over the peak in the setting sun take their color from my mourning sleeves?
Then share this feeling with me, autumn evening wind that pierces me unknown to all.
The flares that show the fishers' work by night seem to have followed my sad boat here.
Is it because you do not know my deep hidden feelings that the flares' light still flickers so?
Waiting in secret for the god's permission, I have passed so many cold years.
If I so much as ask after you with common sympathy, the god may rebuke me for breaking my vow.
I have never forgotten the dew of that time; has the morning glory passed its bloom?
Late in autumn, tangled in the misty hedge, the morning glory fades, barely there at all.
When did this hedge fall into ruin, tangled with mugwort, a snowy old home?
Years have passed, yet I cannot forget our bond: the word you spoke of a parent's parent.
Wait and see in the next life: in this world, is there any case of a child forgetting a parent?
The heart that learned nothing from your old coldness is crueler to me than your coldness itself.
Why should I change now and see you, having heard of such changes of heart in others?
The water among the stones is locked in ice and cannot flow, while the clear moon's light streams across the sky.
On a snowy night when I long for the past, the mandarin duck sleeping on the water adds to my sorrow.
On a lonely winter night of waking, unable to sleep at ease, how short was the tangled dream.
Even if I follow my heart's longing for her, will I lose my way at the river crossing without seeing her shade?
Did you ever think the river waves would turn back, and that I would see your purification end the mourning in wisteria robes?
I thought I had only just put on the wisteria robe of mourning, and now the purification changes the world's current.
At midnight, as wild geese call to one another, the wind over the reeds adds its sad sound.
Should my sleeves, dyed crimson with deep tears, be scorned for the pale green of my rank?
How was the robe between us dyed, that the many colors show me how sad my lot is?
Day and night the sky is darkened with frost and ice, and my tears fall.
Courtier of Toyooka-hime, the goddess in heaven, do not forget the sacred rope my heart has marked.
The dancing maiden too must be grown old, now that the friend of the heavenly sleeves is aged.
Your words make it feel like today, the frost melting on the sacred vine on my sleeves.
Did the sunlight show you my heart, set on the maiden's heavenly feathered sleeves?
The warbler's singing is as it was of old, but the shade of the blossoms we loved has changed.
Even to my dwelling, shut off from the palace by mist, the warbler's voice comes to tell of spring.
In the bamboo flute that has handed down the past, even the singing bird's tune is unchanged.
The warbler sings longing for the past; have the colors of the blossoms it flits among faded?
You who wait for spring in your garden by choice, at least see my autumn leaves carried by the wind.
The autumn leaves scattered by the wind are light; see instead the spring color in the pine on the rock.
Whom do the boatmen long for, that their voices sound so sad off the island of Ōshima?
Out on the open sea, not knowing where we came from or where we go, where should anyone long for you?
If my heart should ever turn from you, I swear by the mirror god of Matsura.
If the prayers of years go wrong, I will think the mirror god cruel.
Rowing away from the island of sorrow, we do not know where we are going or where we will moor.
glosses.note: Uki is 'floating' and 'sorrowful'.

glosses.english: Setting out on a sea road with nothing ahead, I leave my sorrowful self to the wind, rowing away like a boat.
Even the rough Hibiki Sea is nothing beside the pounding of my heart at our troubles.
Had I not sought the two cedars at Hatsuse, would I have met you by the old river?
I know nothing of the old days of the Hatsuse River, but at today's meeting I am swept away.
Though you do not know, seek and you will know: the line of the bur-reed in Mishima Inlet has not broken.
glosses.note: Suji, 'line', means both a plant's runner and a family line.

glosses.english: What line am I, a bur-reed of no account, that I should take root in such sorrow?
Longing for her, I am the same as ever, but by what line has this jeweled vine come to me?
Looking at it, I feel resentful: I will send back this Chinese robe, my sleeves wet with tears.
When you speak of sending it back, I think of your night robe spread for one alone.
In the pond's mirror, where the thin ice has melted, our reflections stand side by side, matchless in the world.
In the clear mirror of the pond, our reflections show plainly that they will dwell together ten thousand years.
To one who has spent the years waiting by the pine, let me hear today the warbler's first song.
glosses.note: Matsu is 'pine' and 'wait'; the warbler is her daughter.

glosses.english: Though years have passed since we parted, could the warbler forget the song of the pine it left its nest in?
How wonderful: the warbler flitting through the flowers to roost now calls at its old nest in the valley.
Seeking out the spring treetops of my old home, I find flowers beyond the common kind.
When the wind blows, even the flowers of the waves show color: is this the famous Cape of Kerria?
Does the spring pond reach the river at Ide? The kerria on the shore is fragrant to its depths.
In this boat, which needs no search for the turtle-borne mountain of the immortals, let us leave our names as ageless.
In the soft spring sun, the boat glides on, and even the drops from its pole scatter like flowers.
Because my heart is set on the purple flower, I would throw myself into the wisteria pool, and would I regret my name?
glosses.note: Fuji/fuchi: 'wisteria' and 'deep pool'.

glosses.english: Before you throw yourself into the pool, stay by the flowers this spring and see.
Would even a butterfly from the flower garden seem a stranger to the autumn-crickets waiting deep among the grasses?
glosses.note: Answers poem 336: 'waiting for autumn' turns 'waiting for spring' around.

glosses.english: I might gladly follow even a butterfly, if only those layers of golden kerria blossoms did not keep us apart.
You will never know my love, for the water seeping through the rocks shows no color as it seethes.
Will the bamboo shoot I planted deep-rooted in my fence grow up and leave me to its own life?
How could it be now? Why would the young bamboo go seeking the root it grew from?
When I liken you to the scent of the orange blossom on her sleeves, you do not seem a different person.
If you liken me to the scent of the orange blossom on her sleeves, I too may fade like its fruit.
We have not slept together at ease; why should the young grass look so tangled, as if something had happened?
Even the silent insect's fire of longing will not go out when someone puts it out.
glosses.note: Omoi, 'longing', contains hi, 'fire'.

glosses.english: The firefly that burns without a voice must hold a fire of longing deeper than words.
Will even today's iris, growing hidden where no one pulls it, only weep its roots away?
glosses.note: Ne is both 'root' and 'cry'.

glosses.english: Pulled into view, your roots look shallow, weeping without knowing the iris from anything else.
Is today the day you pull the iris by the water, which even your colt will not graze?
When will my colt, which walks beside the grebe, ever be pulled away from the iris?
Overwhelmed by longing, I search the old stories, but none tells of a child who turned against a parent like this.
Search the old stories as I might, there is none of a parent with such a heart in this world.
If he saw the lasting color of the pink, would he come seeking the hedge it grew from?
Who would come seeking the root of the pink that grew by a peasant's hedge?
Young grass of Hitachi Bay, Ikaga Point: how can I meet you, waves of Tago Bay?
Waves of Suma Bay on the sea of Suruga in Hitachi, rise up, pine of Hakozaki!
glosses.note: A deliberately muddled parody of place names.

glosses.english: The smoke of love that rises with the cresset flames is a fire that never dies in this world.
If it is smoke that goes with the cresset flames, let it vanish into the empty sky.
Even the wind that passes over the reed leaves seems to pierce my lonely body alone.
In the wild blowing wind, the maidenflower feels it may wither and die.
If the maidenflower bent to the dew below, it would not wither in the wild wind.
Even on an evening of wind and tangled clouds, I never stop thinking of you, whom I cannot forget.
Today, follow the old tracks of the pheasant rising on snowy Mount Oshio.
In the pine woods of Mount Oshio deep in snow, will there be no tracks for today's royal outing?
glosses.note: Miyuki is 'deep snow' and 'royal outing'.

glosses.english: On a morning clouded with snow that soon melted, could I see the light in the sky clearly?
The light shines unclouded in the sky; why did you let the snow blind your eyes?
Whichever way you take it, she is the inner tray of the jeweled comb box, never apart from me.
It is myself I blame, Chinese robe, thinking that I am never near your sleeve.
Chinese robe, again a Chinese robe, Chinese robe, over and over a Chinese robe.
How hateful, the fisher who hid by the rocks until she dived for the jeweled seaweed offshore.
I saw her as driftweed washed onto this beach with nowhere to go, which no fisher came to look for.
Have pity on the purple trousers flower, worn by dew on the same moor, if only as a pretext.
If it were dew from a moor far off, the pale purple might be your pretext.
Not knowing the deep path of Mount Imose, I stumbled lost on the Bridge of Odae.
glosses.note: Imose means 'brother and sister' and 'lovers'.

glosses.english: Not knowing you were lost, all of us stumbled unsure on the paths of Mount Imose.
If I were of no account, I would shun it; how fleeting to stake my life on the ninth month.
Even when you see the morning sunlight, do not let it melt the frost on the bamboo grass.
I feel such sorrow at the thought of forgetting you; what am I to do?
Even the hollyhock that turns to the light by its own will does not melt the morning frost itself.
You did not draw water from the River of Crossing with me, and yet I never promised its shallows to another.
Before I cross the River of Three Shallows, how I wish to vanish like foam on the stream of tears.
On a snowy night, my heart lost in the sky, my sleeves spread for one alone are cold.
Sitting alone with a burning heart, I saw that smoldering flame of longing.
When I am stirred by my troubles, the smoke smolders and rises higher in many ways.
Though I leave my home now, beloved cypress pillar, do not forget me.
Even if it remembers you as beloved, why should the cypress pillar make us stay?
The water among the stones is shallow, yet it stays clear; is it you who will leave the house?
In any case the water among the rocks is frozen; I do not think it will keep my reflection.
How jealous this spring, of the birds who share wings in the deep mountain trees.
Why did I set my heart on the purple, which is so hard to bring near, and dye it so deep?
Not knowing what shade the purple would be, I took care with how it was dyed.
If mist divides the palace, will not even the scent of the plum blossom reach me this much?
At least send this much on the wind, though I have no scent fit to stand among those blossoms.
In the steady spring rain of these calm days, how do you long for the one at your old home?
My sleeves wet by the drops from the eaves as I gaze, how could I not long for you, fleeting as foam?
Though the middle road of Ide unexpectedly divides us, I love you silently, kerria blossom.
glosses.note: Kuchinashi, the kerria's yellow dye, also means 'without a mouth'.

glosses.english: I cannot see the egg that hatched in the same nest; whose hand holds it now?
Hidden in the nest, a gosling of no account: where could anyone take and hide it?
If you drift on the wave road with nowhere to moor, boat of the offing, show me your harbor and I will pole my way to you.
Even a boatman with nowhere to moor would not go along the rocks where he never meant to, though the wind blows.
The flowers' scent does not stay on the bare branch, but it will not stain your sleeves only faintly.
I set my heart all the more on the flowering branch, though I hide its scent for fear of blame.
With the warbler's song, my heart will wander all the more from the flowers I have loved.
This spring, do not neglect this house of flowers, until both colors and scent rub off on you.
Keep blowing the bamboo flute through the night, until even the warbler's roosting branch bends.
Should I blow on a flowering tree the wind kindly spares, until even the birds take fright?
If only the mist did not divide the moon and the flowers, even the roosting bird would burst into song.
If I bring home the flowers' scent rubbed off on these fine sleeves, my wife may suspect me.
How the people at home will wait to see you, coming back in a brocade of flowers.
Coldness has become the way of this sad world; am I alone in not forgetting?
Forgetting what was hard to forget, saying it was the end: is that a heart that bends to the world?
Will you not come at twilight, when the wisteria at my house is deep in color, to find what is left of spring?
I might be at a loss to pick the wisteria, if it is so hard to see in the twilight.
I will lay the blame on purple: the wisteria flower bloomed later than the pine, though it vexed me.
After so many springs heavy with dew, have I come at last to the time the flower opens?
The wisteria flower that rivals a maiden's sleeves: may its color grow deeper with the one who sees it.
How did the river mouth let out the shallow rumor? How did the barrier's rough fence leak?
Do not lay it all on the shallow river mouth; it was the Kukita barrier that leaked.
Do not blame me if my hands, tired of secretly wringing my sleeves, now show their drops today.
What is it, the plant you wear in your hair today? Though I see it, I am dazed.
The one who plucked the laurel would know the name of the plant you wear in your hair, though you cannot tell it.
Did you ever think the young green chrysanthemum, by a drop of dew, would turn deep purple?
A chrysanthemum famous in the garden from its first two leaves: no dew could tell its pale color.
You, spring water dripping from the rocks, keeper of this house, do you know where the one I knew has gone?
Not even the shade of the one who is gone appears, yet the little spring water goes on carefree.
No wonder the old tree of that time has rotted: even the little pine planted then is mossy now.
We trust in the shade of both, the pines whose roots have twined since their first two leaves.
Even the chrysanthemums by the fence, deepening in color, must long for the autumn you wore them on your sleeves.
The chrysanthemum blending with the purple clouds looks like a star in an unclouded reign.
Even a villager through many autumns of drizzle has never seen autumn leaves like these.
Do you see them as ordinary autumn leaves, this brocade in the garden following an ancient precedent?
Worn as it is, handing down the past to now, this jeweled little comb has grown hallowed with age.
May I see you wear it next, until the boxwood comb grows hallowed through ten thousand ages.
Bringing with me the little pines putting out young leaves on the moor, I pray today for the rock they rose from.
Drawn by the long years of the little pines, the young herbs of the moor too will gather years.
How far I trusted the future, in a world that changes before our eyes.
Life may end, but not the bond between us, unlike the common bonds of an uncertain world.
Though no distance on the road divides us, my heart is troubled by this morning's light snow.
Fleeting, I may vanish into the empty sky, like light spring snow drifting on the wind.
The heart that stays in the world I have turned from is the tether on the mountain path I enter.
If you worry about the world you turn from, do not cut the tether you cannot leave behind.
After the long years between us, the barrier of Meeting is so hard to pass that my tears fall.
Only my tears flow from the spring, unchecked by the barrier; the road where we would meet was cut off long ago.
Though I sank once and have not forgotten, unrepentant I could throw myself again into the waves of wisteria at your house.
glosses.note: Kori-zuma: 'unrepentant', with Suma, where he was exiled.

glosses.english: The pool you would throw yourself into is no true pool; would you still be drenched again by the unrepentant waves?
Has autumn come close to me? Even as I watch, the green-leaved mountain changes color.
The waterbird's green feathers never change color, but beneath the bush clover the look of things is different.
Who would blame the old fisherwoman, dripping with brine, who rises with the waves of age on a shore that rewards her?
With the brine-wet fisherwoman as my guide on the wave road, I would like to visit that rush hut on the beach.
Even one who left the world to live on Akashi Bay could not clear away the darkness of a parent's heart.
Dawn is near, when the light will rise; now at last I tell the dream I saw long ago.
Why does the warbler, flitting from flower to flower, not choose the cherry above all to roost in?
How could even the box-bird roosting in deep mountain trees ever tire of the flowers' color?
Watching from afar, I grieve much that I cannot pick the cherry, yet I long for the flower in the evening light.
Do not show it now, mountain cherry, that you set your heart on picking a flower beyond your reach.
I tame you as a keepsake of the one I long for; why, little cat, do you cry so?
glosses.note: Ne o naku: the cat's mewing, also 'weeping'.

glosses.english: Who else knows my heart and will speak with the pine of Sumiyoshi that has outlived the age of gods?
Today even the old fisherwoman knows the shore of Sumiyoshi, where living has been worth it.
I cannot forget the past, when I see the sign of the god of Sumiyoshi.
glosses.note: Matsu is 'pine' and 'first of all'.

glosses.english: The frost that falls late at night on the pines of Suminoe: is it a sacred cord the god has hung?
Frost late at night adds sacred cords to the sakaki leaves held in the hand of the god's servant.
The frost that mingles with the priests' sacred cords: surely it is a clear sign from the god.
Day and night, not knowing the sky I rise and leave into, what dew is it that soaks my sleeve?
Let this wretched self vanish into the sky of dawn and dusk, so it ends as only a dream.
How I regret the sin I committed: the heartvine was not a hair ornament the gods allowed me.
glosses.note: Aoi, 'heartvine', also sounds like 'day of meeting'.

glosses.english: Why did I pick up the fallen leaf of the double vine? Its name is dear, as a hair ornament.
I myself have become something else, yet you, feigning not to know me, are still yourself.
Can I hope to stay a while, when I only cling for a moment like the dew on a lotus leaf?
Let us vow, if not in this world, to share a lotus leaf; do not keep your heart apart from me like separate dewdrops.
Do you mean for my sleeves to be wet with evening dew, rising to leave as you hear the evening cicada?
How will she hear it, waiting in her house? The evening cicada's voice troubles my heart both ways.
Could I hear of your life as a nun as someone else's matter, when I too dripped brine on the shore of Suma?
glosses.note: Ama is 'nun' and 'fisherfolk'.

glosses.english: How could you have been left behind by the nun's boat, you who fished on Akashi Bay?
Now at the end, even my smoke as I burn will be tangled, with the fire of longing that never ends still left.
I would rise beside you and vanish, in a contest of smoke over our tangled sorrows.
Even if I become smoke in the sky with nowhere to go, I will never leave the place I long for.
If someone asks in whose day the seed was sown, how will the pine on the rock answer, unable to speak?
glosses.note: Iwane is 'rock' and 'unspoken'.

glosses.english: When the season comes, it blooms in unchanged color, even the cherry at this house whose branch has withered.
This spring I string tears like beads on the willow buds, not knowing where the scattered flowers have gone.
Wet with the drops beneath the tree, it is upside down: a spring when I wear the robe of mist.
glosses.note: The father mourns his son: the order of mourning is reversed.

glosses.english: Even the dead would not have thought you should wear the evening mist, leaving you behind.
How bitter: for whom should we wear the robe of mist, when the flower fell before spring was over?
If so, let me grow close to the branch already grown close, with leave from the god who guards the leaves.
Though no god guarding the leaves dwells in the oak, is this the house where anyone may grow close to the treetops?
Though I part from the world before you on the path we enter, come seek the same place too.
Longing for a place that is not this wretched world, my heart enters the mountain path of renunciation.
Though I do not forget the bitter joint, this child of the black bamboo is hard to throw away.
glosses.note: Fushi: 'bamboo joint' and 'occasion'; ko: 'child'.

glosses.english: Saying nothing says more than words, more than any koto: I see that in your shy look.
Of this deep night, I understood only the sorrow; could I play anything more than that on the koto, more than words?
glosses.note: Koto is both 'words' and 'zither'.

glosses.english: In this house of dewy weeds, the insects' voices are unchanged from autumns long ago.
The tune of the flute is unchanged, but the sound of the one who is gone never ends in my heart.
If wind blows on this bamboo flute, I would pass its sound down to a long line of descendants.
glosses.note: Ne is 'sound' and 'root'; yo, 'joint' and 'generation'.

glosses.english: We vowed to share a lotus seat, yet today, when we part like dewdrops, is so sad.
Though you vow without a barrier a house of lotus, your heart will not settle there with me.
I knew autumn was bitter in general, yet the bell cricket's voice is hard to shake off.
glosses.note: Furi-sute: 'shake off', with furi, the bell's shaking.

glosses.english: Though you shun your lodging in the grass by your own will, the bell cricket's voice never grows old.
Even to a dwelling far beyond the clouds, the autumn night's moon does not forget to come.
The moon looks the same in the cloud-high sky, yet my house's autumn is changed.
In the evening mist that deepens the sadness of this mountain village, I feel I have no sky to set out into.
Even the mist rising round the peasant's fence will not hold a man whose heart is in the sky.
Am I alone to be the example of one who knows the sad world, letting my soaked sleeves rot my name?
Even if I did not put the wet robe of false rumor on you, could the name of rotted sleeves be hidden?
glosses.note: Nureginu, 'wet robe', means 'false accusation'.

glosses.english: Soaked by the dew from the eaves on the reed plain, must I push through the mist rising eightfold?
Do you mean to use as your pretext the dew on the grass you push through, and put the wet robe on me again?
I left my soul behind in your cold sleeve, and by my own heart I am lost.
If you block it, it will look shallow: if you cannot dam the name that flows like a mountain river.
Where on this moor of drooping maidenflowers did you take a lodging only for one night?
I pushed through the thick grass of the autumn moor, but I did not tie a pillow for a brief sleep.
How can I comfort you, knowing this sorrow? Do you long for the living, or grieve for the dead?
Which should I grieve for, in a world where I do not see even the dew that vanishes as belonging to the grass?
Far from home, I pushed through the bamboo plains of Ono, and like the deer I do not spare my voice.
glosses.note: Shika is 'deer' and 'thus'.

glosses.english: The mountain dwellers in wisteria mourning robes, in this dewy autumn, add their cries to the deer's calling.
In the pond water where the one I knew no longer dwells, does the autumn night's moon lodge alone?
When should I wake you? From a dream on a night that never dawns, was that what she said, that single word?
On Mount Ono, crying out morning and evening, my endless tears are the Silent Falls.
glosses.note: Otonashi, 'soundless', for weeping without a sound.

glosses.english: I would mingle with the smoke that rose up to the peak, not bending in a direction I do not wish.
A keepsake that cannot comfort my longing: the jeweled box clouded with tears.
Bitter and weary, on a winter night when my heart will not open, the rock door of the barrier shuts tighter still.
Rather than resent the self you have grown used to, I might change into the robes of a fisher of Matsushima.
glosses.note: She means becoming a nun.

glosses.english: Because the wet robe of the fisher of Matsushima is worn, should the name be given out that she changed it?
Is there a bond? Keeping you in my heart, I feel pity, and I hear you resent me.
Why do I, one person of no account, hear myself called wretched and also pitied?
If I counted for anything, I would know the world's sorrow for myself; instead I wet my sleeves for another.
I pitied others for the world's sorrow, but never thought it would take my own place.
Though I do not mourn this self, how sad that, at the end, the firewood will run out.
glosses.note: Firewood running out recalls the Buddha's death.

glosses.english: Today, the first day of cutting firewood for the Law, begins a long road to the Law we pray for.
Though the rite must end, I trust in the bond we tie through this Law, from life to life.
The bond we tied will not break, though few of us are left for the rite of the Law.
So brief, that I see it settle: the dew on the bush clover, scattered by the wind.
In this world of dew, ever racing to vanish, let us not be long apart, the one before, the one behind.
Who would see the world of dew, which the autumn wind lets rest for no moment, as only on the grass leaves?
I long for that autumn evening of old; now, in dawn and dusk, the dream of her last moment.
Even that autumn of old feels like now, and more dew settles on my wet sleeves.
The dew of tears feels neither old nor new; every autumn night is simply hard.
Did she dislike the withered moor, so that she set no heart on autumn?
Though she rose into the clouds, look back, for my own autumn is not over, in this changing world.
At my house no one makes much of the flowers; why have you come searching for spring?
Following the scent I came in vain, if you call it only a visit for the flowers.
Thinking I would melt like snow in this sad world, against my will I live on as it falls.
At a house whose master who planted and watched the flowers is gone, the warbler comes and sings as if it does not know.
Must it now fall to ruin, the spring hedge she who is gone set her heart on?
Weeping, I went home like the wild geese: in this passing world, no place is an everlasting land.
glosses.note: Kari: 'passing' and 'wild goose'.

glosses.english: Since the seedbed water where the wild geese passing through stayed ran dry, I cannot even see the flowers reflected.
Today, changing into summer robes, will not old thoughts rise up?
From today, when the robes change to light feathery ones, this world of the cicada shell is sadder still.
Water plants may well grow in the water I lean on, but today I have even forgotten the name of the heartvine.
I thought I had mostly cast off the world, yet should I pick the heartvine, which means 'meeting'?
Did you come wet from the passing rain, mountain cuckoo, on this night I mourn the dead?
Cuckoo, give him the message: at the old home, the orange blossom is in full bloom now.
Through the long summer day I spend weeping, the insects' voices seem to blame me.
Seeing the fireflies that know the night is sad: my longing burns at every hour.
I watch the Weaver's meeting from beyond the clouds, and in my garden of parting the dew settles more.
My tears of longing for you have no end; why do they call today the end of mourning?
I who long for her am coming to my end, yet so many tears are left.
The white dew on the chrysanthemums we tended together falls this autumn on my sleeve alone.
Phantom who passes through the great sky, seek where the soul has gone who does not come even in my dreams.
The court people hurry today to the Harvest Feast; I have spent it not knowing the sun's light.
Longing for the one who crossed the Mountain of Death, I see her traces and am lost still more.
It is no use gathering and reading these letters; become smoke in the same clouds as she did, seaweed of brine.
glosses.note: Moshiogusa, 'salt seaweed', stands for written letters.

glosses.english: Not knowing if I will live to spring, today I wear in my hair the plum that colors in the snow.
I prayed for flowers to see a thousand springs, while I myself grew old as the snow fell.
glosses.note: Furu is 'fall' and 'grow old'.

glosses.english: Lost in grief, not knowing the months pass, have the year and my life both ended today?
So uncertain: whom can I ask how I came to be, I who know neither my beginning nor my end?
Should the warbler not come at once to the garden plum whose scent the wind has kindly carried?
If I were one to be lured by the flowers' scent, would I let the wind's message pass me by?
If your sleeves, fragrant from the root, should brush the flowers, they too may spread a matchless name.
If I follow the flowers' scent to the house that sends it, people may blame me for loving color.
Show a little color, first plum blossom, to see if picking you makes your scent all the sweeter.
From afar you may judge it dry wood, but the first plum blossom is fragrant underneath.
Everyone must be turning their hearts to the flowers, while I alone am lost in the spring night's dark.
Perhaps it is the season: the plum blossom knows sorrow, but it does not turn its heart just because of this.
With that single phrase of Bamboo River we struck up, did you know the depth of my heart?
glosses.note: Fushi is 'bamboo joint' and 'melody'.

glosses.english: We hurried to Bamboo River so as not to let the night grow late; what phrase should I have kept in mind?
Because of the cherry, my heart is troubled by the wind, though I see the flowers as heartless.
Since they are flowers that fall as soon as they bloom, I feel no deep grudge at losing.
For flowers to fall in the wind is the way of the world; I could not watch calmly as they faded on the branch.
Flowers falling willingly by the pond's edge, even if you turn to foam, drift to our side.
Though the wind of the great sky scatters them, I gather the cherry flowers and look on them as ours.
Is there a sleeve wide enough to cover the cherry flowers, so their many-hued glow will not be scattered?
Counting the months and days that pass with your coldness, how bitter this end of spring.
Well then, why is it that nothing goes the way of one of no account, but a heart determined not to lose to others?
How unreasonable: how can one leave to a single heart winning and losing, which go by strength?
Take pity and let my hand go free, if I am one who leaves life and death to you.
Gazing at flowers I spent the spring; from today, am I to wander lost beneath thick grief?
Today I learn it, from the look of you gazing at the sky, that you had turned your heart to the flowers.
To what sort of person should one give that single word, 'pity', in this changing world?
Since life and death in this living world do not go as I wish, shall I end without hearing your single word?
If wisteria flowers were something to hold in my hand, would I see color finer than the pine's?
Purple colors are akin, but the wisteria flower would not hang upon my heart.
Do you remember that night of Bamboo River, though there was no phrase to treasure?
At Bamboo River, where trust flowed on in vain, I have learned this world is a sorry place.
Why have I been left behind in this passing world, by the waterbird that cast me off and flew away?
glosses.note: Kari no ko: 'goose eggs' and 'passing world'.

glosses.english: When I wonder how we came to leave the nest like this, I know the sad fate of the floating waterbird.
Weeping as he spreads his wings over us: without you, I would have ended as the egg left in the nest.
The one I knew and my house both went up in smoke; why did I alone stay unvanished?
My heart weary of the world goes back and forth to the mountains, but do you keep me off with eightfold clouds?
Though my heart is not clear of the world with all tracks cut off, I have borrowed a lodging on the mountain of Uji.
glosses.note: Uji puns on ushi, 'sad': 'mountain of a sad world'.

glosses.english: More senselessly fragile than the dew on leaves endlessly blown by the mountain wind are my tears.
At dawn I cannot see the road home; Mount Maki, which I came to seek, is shrouded in mist.
The autumn mist keeps off the path along the peak where clouds rest, all the more at this season.
Trying to fathom the lady at the bridge, I dip my pole into the shallows; its falling drops have soaked my sleeves.
Pushing back and forth along the Uji River, will the drops of morning and evening wear your sleeves away entirely?
Sadder than you, who turn from the world before my eyes, is my soul, which parts from you far away.
If I lived, I could see that it is him: the old age of the pine I left on the rock, known to none.
The mountain wind can be heard blowing the mist apart, yet the white waves across the distance still seem to keep us apart.
Though waves separate the shores on either side, keep blowing between us, wind over the Uji River.
Coming in search of the place where mountain cherries glow, I have picked the same blossoms for my hair.
Spring traveler, on your way to pick flowers for your hair, you passed by the peasant's hedge.
Though without me the grass hut fall to ruin, I believe this single word will not wither.
In what world could the grass hut wither, where we tied a long night's bond?
What must the autumn mountain village be like this evening, as deer call and dew gathers on the little bush clover?
In this mountain village shrouded in a mist of tears, the deer at the fence cry out together, voice answering voice.
Do you think I hear only as common sorrow the cry of the deer whose mate is lost in the morning mist?
Even seeing the color change in the reeds, I think of your sleeves worn in ink-dyed mourning.
My sleeves, changed in color, have become the lodging of dew; there is no place left for myself.
In the sky where autumn mist will not clear, why must you tell me again that this world is passing?
Since you have gone and the rocky path is cut off, how should I look on the snow upon the pine?
If only I could think of the one who vanished as snow piled on the pine needles deep in the mountains.
On the mountain bridge deep in snow, I see no other tracks but yours treading back and forth.
Shall I cross first, as your guide, the mountain stream where my horse tramples the icicles closed over it?
The oak I trusted to stand in the shade of has become an empty bed.
If you had been here to see the bracken of the peak, I might have known it as a sign of spring.
For whom shall I pick the little parsley by the snowy shore and make much of it, being without a parent?
This spring I would pick for my hair, without mist between us, the cherry of that house I saw through others.
Where will you search to pick it, the cherry of a house shrouded in mist and gray mourning?
Let us tie a long promise into the trefoil knot, our strands coming together at a single place.
On a fragile string of tear-pearls I cannot even thread together, how could I tie a promise that must last so long?
This dawn gathers together voice after voice that tell the sorrow of the mountain village.
I thought these mountains so deep not even birds' voices were heard, yet the world's sorrows came seeking us.
I would ask the mountain princess who dyed one branch differently: which color is deeper?
I cannot tell the mind of the mountain princess who dyes it, but the fading side may be the deeper one.
Guarding the great moor where the maidenflowers bloom, are you narrow-hearted, tying up a rope?
The maidenflower on the misty morning plain: one who sets a heart on it sees it.
Having been the guide, am I to be the one lost on a road of dawn and dusk my heart does not go along?
Think of a heart passing the days in many troubles, if you are lost on a road of your own making.
Do you think it common, my pushing through the bamboo grass on a road deep in dew?
Though you may not say I wore your night robe and grew close, you cannot wholly deny the pretext.
Hearts without a barrier may pass to each other, but I will not call them sleeves grown close.
It is not that the bond will break; will the Lady of the Bridge, her lone sleeve spread, wet it at midnight?
Trusting your 'it will not break', must I wait to cross the long span of the Uji Bridge?
Even the trees I glimpsed once at the height of blossom: are they lonely in autumn?
The cherries teach us that blossoms that bloom and glow, and autumn leaves too, are not lasting in this world.
Where has autumn gone? It is hard to pass by the shade of the autumn leaves in the mountain village.
On the rock wall of the mountain village where the one I knew is gone, the vine creeps on, long-hearted.
Do not blow so hard, pine wind of the peak, on the trees where loneliness deepens as autumn ends.
I do not mean to lie down with the young grass, yet I feel my heart tied in knots.
glosses.note: Ne is 'root' and 'sleep'.

glosses.english: We gaze at the same clouded sky; why does the drizzle add to my unease?
In the deep mountain village where hail falls, the sky we gaze at morning and evening grows dark too.
How sad this dawn: the plovers by the frost-cold shore cry out in misery.
The plover crying as it shakes off dawn frost: does it know the heart of one lost in grief?
In the deep mountains, clouded over with no sunlight seen, my heart too is darkened these days.
Even my tears that fall crimson are useless, since they cannot dye the color of a keepsake.
I long to follow the moon traveling the sky, not to be left behind, since this is no world to stay in.
Sick with longing, I wish for medicine to die; shall I vanish into the Snow Mountains?
Even recalling the past is futile; why trust anything for the future?
If you think the future short, at least do not turn against me before my eyes.
These are the first bracken shoots, which do not forget their custom, since I picked them many springs for you.
This spring, whom shall I show them to, the little bracken of the peak, picked as a keepsake of the dead?
Is it a flower akin to the heart of the one who picks it, glowing beneath without showing its color?
One should have picked with a careful heart the flower used as a pretext by the one who sees it.
How fleeting: on the island where you rise from the robe of mist, the season of flowers untying has come.
In the mountain village, where even those who see it are lost in storms, there is a flower scent that recalls the past.
The plum my sleeves brushed keeps its unchanged scent, but is the house different, now that its roots have moved away?
If I threw myself into the river of tears that runs ahead of me, my life would not lag behind theirs.
Though I throw myself and sink in the river of tears, I will not forget in each shallow of longing.
Everyone seems to hurry off, while on the bay of my sleeve one fisher-nun alone drips with brine.
Is it different from the fisher's brine-dripping robe? My sleeve is wet on the floating waves.
Living on, I came to a shallow of joy; what if I had thrown myself into the river of Uji?
I do not forget the past and its longing, but today my heart goes on ahead in hope.
As I gaze, even the moon that left the mountains, weary of the world, goes back into the mountains.
Like a boat rowing on the shining Lake of Grebes, though not under full sail, we did meet.
If it were a flower glowing by an ordinary hedge, I would have picked it as I pleased.
The chrysanthemum in the garden, withered by the frost, still keeps its lingering color unfaded.
I watch them, flowers that cling while the settled dew has not vanished: will they keep only this morning's color?
I should have seen it as a likeness: the morning glory, on which the white dew's bond was laid.
The flower withers before the dew vanishes; more fleeting still is the dew left behind.
Even the moon of the great sky lodges at my house, but you, past the waiting evening, do not appear.
Even in the shade of pines in my mountain village, there was never an autumn wind that pierced me like this.
The maidenflower droops all the more: what morning dew settled on it, leaving this trace?
I might have heard it as ordinary, but the evening cicada's voice is bitter this autumn dusk.
What a pity for your name, that you grew familiar with the barrier river the world will never let you cross.
The barrier river looks shallow on the surface, but does its flow underneath ever stop?
Thick is the dew on the road I pushed through in vain; the autumn sky recalls the past.
I take into myself the scent from your robe and sleeves grown close to another, and resent it.
I trusted the robe between us, sleeves grown close, yet will we come so far apart over this much?
Should you resent in one strand alone the inner sash, tied in a different bond?
If I did not remember lodging beneath the mistletoe, how lonely my traveler's sleep beneath this tree would be.
glosses.note: Yadorigi, 'mistletoe', also means 'having lodged'.

glosses.english: How sad that you think of the foot of this ruined, rotten tree as the mistletoe where you once lodged.
The bamboo pampas grass, its sleeves beckoning thick with dew, seems lost in thoughts it will not show in plumes.
Even the look of the moor at autumn's end I know only through the wind faintly stirring the pampas grass.
Picking wisteria to be an ornament for the emperor's hair, I hung my sleeve on a branch beyond my reach.
Since it is a flower whose scent will last ten thousand ages, I see its color today as one I cannot tire of.
The ornament picked for your hair: are its flowers not equal to the purple clouds?
It looks no ordinary color, the waves of wisteria flowers that have risen to the clouds above.
Wondering if her voice will be like the face-bird's I heard of, I push through the thickets to seek her today.
If she is a likeness of the one I knew, I will keep her by me as a cleansing doll for each shallow of longing.
glosses.note: Nademono: a doll that takes on one's sins and is set adrift.

glosses.english: Who would trust as a shadow by their side a cleansing doll set adrift in each shallow of the purification river?
The little bush clover is roped off and safe; by what dew do its lower leaves change color?
Had I known it grew at the foot of Miyagino's bush clover, the dew would not have made distinctions.
How simply happy I would be, if I could think it a place not of this world.
Even if I seek a place not of this sad world, I wish for some way to see you in your prime.
Why did the spring water that never runs dry not keep at least the face of the one who is gone?
Are the weeds so thick that bar the door? The rain drips on too long at this eastern house.
When I see it as a keepsake, my sleeves grow wet, overflowing as the morning dew.
The mistletoe has changed color this autumn, but the moon shines clear as of old.
Even the village name is as of old, but the moon in the bedroom shows a changed face.
Though it is not yet old, know that for you it waits with a deep heart.
glosses.note: Matsu: 'pine' and 'wait'.

glosses.english: Though I promise a long age, what is still sad is a life that does not know tomorrow.
I would not grieve my heart, if only life were the one uncertain thing in this world.
I must wander lost as never before, with tears running ahead and darkening the road.
How can I, unable to stop my tears with my narrow sleeves, hold back our parting?
The long bond of the Uji Bridge will not decay; do not trouble your heart about its weakness.
The Uji Bridge, so unsafe with only gaps: do you say I should trust it will not decay?
Though years pass, will it change, the heart I vow to you at the cape of Orange Islet?
The color of Orange Islet may not change, but this drifting boat does not know where it will go.
glosses.note: Ukifune, 'drifting boat', is her name.

glosses.english: Pushing through snow on the peak and ice at the shore, I am lost over you, though not lost on the road.
More than the snow that falls in flurries and freezes at the shore, I will vanish midway in the sky.
How miserable these days, when even the sky goes dark until I cannot see the clouds over where you are.
How is it in the village beyond the swelling waters, in these days darkened by gazing that never clears?
Knowing that the village's name applies to me, the crossing at Uji in Yamashiro is all the harder to live in.
glosses.note: Uji puns on ushi, 'sad'.

glosses.english: I wish I could become a rain cloud on the dark peak that never clears, drifting through life.
Idly, the rain that teaches me my place never stops, and my sleeves swell with water too.
Not knowing that waves were crossing, I thought only that the pine of Sue would wait for me.
glosses.note: Waves over Sue's Pine Mountain mean a faithless lover.

glosses.english: Where shall I throw myself away? I go weeping, and no mountain is without white clouds.
Even if, worn by grief, I throw myself away, I fear leaving a shameful name after I am gone.
If I leave not even my body in this sad world, where will you go to grieve for my grave?
Think rather that we will meet again later; do not lose your heart in this world's dream.
Adding my weeping to the dying echo of the bell, tell her my life has ended.
Do you too weep in secret, cuckoo, bird of the Mountain of Death? If our hearts are joined it is all in vain.
Near where the orange blossom is fragrant, the cuckoo should take care when it weeps.
glosses.note: Kaoru, 'fragrant', is also his rival's name.

glosses.english: If I too let the old home fall to ruin, who will love the shade of the mistletoe where we lodged?
My heart that knows sorrow is behind no one's, but being of no account, I live on vanishing.
Even I, sad as I am and seeing the world as changing, do I grieve so others know?
Even the autumn wind that ties dew on the reed leaves pierces me most in the evening.
Though I mingle on the moor where the maidenflowers sway, could the dew's fickle name be laid on me?
When called a flower, its name is fickle, but does the maidenflower sway for every dew?
Spend a night and test it again: will the maidenflower change in the color of its prime or not?
If you lend me lodging I would sleep a night, though my heart does not turn to ordinary flowers.
I saw her there, but could not take her in my hand; when I look again, the mayfly is gone, I know not where.
Who laid a weir across the swift shallows of the river of tears I threw myself into, and held me back?
Even if I go on living like this in the sad world, who would know of it in the city of the moon?
Do not bend in the wind of Adashino, maidenflower; I will rope you off, though the road is far.
I transplanted it and grieve over the maidenflower, to a grass hut that has turned from the sad world.
I came seeking the pine cricket's voice, yet again I am lost in the dew of the bush clover field.
Hunting robe that came through the dew of autumn fields, do not blame the house deep in weeds.
One who does not see the deep night's moon as moving: does he not stay at this house near the mountain rim?
I will gaze at the moon until it sets behind the mountain rim, to see if the bedroom's planks show any sign.
The past I cannot forget: even the bamboo flute's painful notes bring my weeping out.
glosses.note: Fushi: 'bamboo joint' and 'melody'.

glosses.english: At the sound of the flute I too yearned for the past, and my sleeves were wet when you left.
Living on so fleetingly in the sad shallows of Furu River, I do not wish to seek the twin cedars.
glosses.note: Furu: the river's name and 'to live on'.

glosses.english: I do not know the root of the cedar at Furu River, but I see you as a likeness of the one who passed.
My heart does not single out autumn evenings, yet dew is scattered on my gazing sleeves.
The deep sorrow of an autumn night in the mountain village is known by one who broods.
I live on without knowing the world is sad, yet people knew me as one who broods.
Thinking of myself and others as gone, I have cast off again the world I once cast off.
The world I had come to think was at its end, I have turned from it again and again.
I hurry, not to miss the fisher's boat that must be rowing far from shore.
glosses.note: Ama is 'nun' and 'fisherfolk'.

glosses.english: My heart leaves the shore of the sad world, but the fisher's floating log does not know where it goes.
At the foot of the mountain the winter wind blew over, there is not even shade to hide in.
I think no one will wait for me, yet looking at the treetops of the mountain village it is hard to pass.
You have turned from the ordinary world, yet it is I who suffer, thinking it a way to shun me.
Even gazing at the snow darkening the moors and mountains, what has passed is sad today.
Picking the young herbs between the snow in the mountain village and making much of them, I still trust in your future.
From now on, even the young herbs of the snowy moor will gather years for you.
I cannot see the one whose sleeves brushed me, but the flower scent glows like his in the spring dawn.
On the water where the one I knew left not even a shadow, my falling tears cannot be dammed.
Now that I have changed into a nun's robe, shall I keep my sleeve as a keepsake of the past and long for it?
Taking the road I sought to the teacher of the Law as my guide, I am lost on a mountain I never expected.
